items.title: Danny Barker Interview, 1959-06-30
items.q: He was after John E. J., I think between him and George Gennon.

ctx.x: John E. J., was that the other one?
No, no, it was another one. He was after John E. J., I think between him and George Gennon. John E. J. J. J. I'll find a guy. He was terrific. Terrific.
What kind of a beat did they feature? Did they feature a straight four or two?

items.title: George Guesnon Interview
items.q: You take Manuel Sales, Danny Barker, myself, Poissy Sevier, Hendrick Kimball. All them men I'm telling you about were all good banjo players. And all of us got a knowledge of learning from each other.

ctx.x: There's another thing I remember you've talked about, which we never did get on tape, that you're not ashamed to ask people questions to show you something. Whereas some musicians will try to act like they know it all already, and they're ashamed, you know, to ask somebody to show them anything. But you say, in the old days, you'd get together and you'd watch somebody and show me how to do that.

Well, you see, Bill, those days, that was the basic conception of music. Because you take all the great players around you, let's put it to that. Because, in fact, there was no such a thing as a great New Orleans musician. There was no such a thing. Some guys knew music. Some guys could read pretty well. But you couldn't put them in the class of a master musician. They were master players. In other words, they're dependent on learning the basic fundamentals of their instrument first. Know your instrument. That…
If I remember rightly now, it's coming to me a little bit. It seems like you said once, Glennie said, if you're going to ask somebody, don't ask a damn fool the question. Oh, yeah.
